what_its_for: Thiothixene is used to treat schizophrenia, a mental health condition that can cause you to hear, see, or believe things that are not real. It helps reduce symptoms like hallucinations (hearing or seeing things that are not there), delusions (believing things that are not true), and confused or disorganized thinking. It works by balancing certain chemicals in the brain.
how_to_take: Take thiothixene exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the capsules whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better, as stopping suddenly can cause symptoms to come back or cause withdrawal effects.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition and how you respond to the medicine. Doses are usually taken 2 to 3 times a day. Common starting doses are low and your doctor may slowly increase the dose over time. Never take more than prescribed. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store thiothixene at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine in its original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and make side effects worse. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do activities that require you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you, since it can cause drowsiness. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated — be careful in hot weather, during exercise, or in hot baths, as this medicine can affect your body's ability to cool down. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause dizziness or lightheadedness. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as many drugs can interact with thiothixene.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: uncontrolled muscle movements in your face, tongue, or body (this could be a serious condition called tardive dyskinesia); muscle stiffness, high fever, fast heartbeat, or confusion (signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); severe dizziness or fainting; difficulty swallowing or breathing; chest pain or irregular heartbeat; signs of infection like fever or sore throat; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual bleeding or bruising; thoughts of harming yourself or others; or a seizure. Also call your doctor if your symptoms do not improve or get worse.
when_it_works: Thiothixene does not work right away. Some improvement in sleep, agitation, or anxiety may be noticed within the first few days. However, it may take several weeks — usually 2 to 6 weeks or longer — to feel the full benefit of this medicine. It is very important to keep taking it even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults: Older patients, especially those with dementia, may have a higher risk of serious side effects including an increased risk of stroke or death. This medicine is generally not recommended for older adults with dementia-related behavior problems. Children: The safety and effectiveness in children has not been well established; use only if directed by a doctor. Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who took this medicine in the third trimester of pregnancy may have muscle movement or withdrawal symptoms after birth. The risks and benefits should be discussed with your doctor. Breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Let your doctor know if you have kidney or liver disease, as dose adjustments may be needed.
